metric_rationale: In this specific experimental design, Take The Best (TTB) will systematically choose the option with the highest-validity discriminating cue, which on the critical conflict trials (trials 1-6) happens to be the option with the *smaller* total number of positive features. The Weighted Additive (WADD) model, being compensatory, will consistently favor the option with the *larger* total number of positive features because the coalition of lower-validity cues outweighs the single highest-validity cue. By calculating the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with fewer positive features, we expect a value near 0.75 for TTB (matching on 6 out of 8 unique trials) and near 0.0 for WADD (which always picks the option with more positive features in this design).

Calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the experimental design explicitly pits a single high-validity cue against a coalition of multiple lower-validity cues on 8 out of 10 trial types, TTB and WADD will make opposing predictions for the majority of the experiment. TTB simulated data will yield a very high proportion (near 1.0, minus noise), whereas WADD simulated data will yield a very low proportion (as the compensatory coalitions will outweigh the single top cue).

This metric isolates the critical trials where Tallying and WADD make diametrically opposed predictions. In these trials, one option has 3 low-validity features while the competing option has 2 high-validity features. Tallying simply counts features and strongly prefers the 3-feature option. WADD weighs features by validity and generally prefers the 2-feature option. The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with Tallying's prediction on these specific trials.

The design includes a crucial reversal between Trial 2 (A=[1,1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,0,1,1,1]) and Trial 3 (A=[0,0,1,1,1] vs B=[1,1,0,0,0]). In Trial 2, Tallying counts 2 positive cues for A and 3 for B, thus predicting a preference for B. WADD, however, values the two highest-validity cues of A (1.0 + 0.8 = 1.8) more than the three lower-validity cues of B (0.6 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.6), predicting a preference for A. Trial 3 is the exact opposite. By computing the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 2 and Trial 3, we expect a strongly negative value for Tallying (which prefers B then A) and a strongly positive value for WADD (which prefers A then B).
